title: SAIL × Baseline Energy Hackathon 2024
summary: A first-place hackathon solution that forecasts electricity consumption with a hybrid CNN-LSTM → XGBoost model.

case.problem: Forecast short-term electricity consumption from real energy data for the UiS × Baseline Energy challenge — under hackathon time pressure, in a two-person team.
case.data: Hourly electricity load paired with temperature — roughly 8,900 hours. I held out the final ~3 weeks as an untouched test set.
case.approach: I framed this as hourly time-series regression: given the last 24 hours of load and weather, predict the next hour — then roll that forward to fill the two blanked validation days. The whole pipeline lives in cnn_lstm_with_xgb.py — I engineer features from the raw load-and-temperature signal (create_features()), slice the series into 24-hour supervised windows (create_sequences()), and train a CNN-LSTM with a custom attention layer to learn the temporal structure. Rather than let the network's own dense head make the final call, I peel off its learned representation and feed it into an XGBoost regressor — the CNN-LSTM → XGBoost hybrid that won the hackathon.

methods.why: Each prediction sees the previous 24 hours, so the model always has a full daily cycle of load and temperature as context.

Demand is strongly periodic. Sine/cosine encodings let the model treat hour 23 and hour 0 — or Sunday and Monday — as neighbours instead of far-apart numbers, while the calendar flags give it weekday context.
Load is autoregressive — the previous hour and the same hour yesterday are strong predictors — and 24-hour rolling means smooth out noise to expose the underlying trend.
Both heating and cooling push demand up, so load versus temperature is U-shaped; the squared term lets the model capture that non-linear relationship.

The 1-D CNN extracts short local patterns (like the morning ramp-up) and compresses the window; the LSTM models longer-range dependencies across the day; and a custom attention layer weights the most informative hours instead of treating all 24 equally.

methods.method: Network as feature extractor, then XGBoost
methods.why: I used the trained network to produce a learned representation and let XGBoost make the final prediction. Gradient boosting is very strong on tabular features, so it sharpens the regression beyond the network's own dense head.

MinMax scaling keeps the 13 features comparable; dropout and batch-norm curb overfitting; and Adam with learning-rate scheduling plus early stopping keeps training stable and ends it at the right time.

title: Medical Emergency Agent
summary: A GraphRAG agent that answers medical-emergency queries over a property-graph knowledge store built from call transcripts.

case.problem: Answer medical-emergency questions reliably by grounding an LLM in real call-transcript data and a medical knowledge graph, rather than letting it hallucinate.
case.data: A corpus of emergency call transcripts, from which I build a property-graph knowledge store plus a vector index for retrieval.
case.approach: This is a GraphRAG system, not a plain chatbot. I extract a medical property graph from the transcripts (PGExtractor.py, dynamicKG_builder.py), index it alongside a vector store, and orchestrate retrieve → reason → answer as an explicit LangGraph flow (graphflow.py). The LLM only answers over what's retrieved from both the graph and the vectors, and a Gradio UI makes it queryable. Built as a Poetry project on LlamaIndex + LangChain/LangGraph.

methods.why: I extract entities and relationships from the transcripts into a property graph, so the agent can reason over structured medical connections rather than loose text.
Vector search finds semantically similar passages while the knowledge graph supplies precise, connected facts — together they ground answers far better than either alone.
Modelling retrieve → reason → answer as an explicit state graph makes the agent controllable and inspectable instead of a black-box prompt chain.
I compared answering from the graph alone against answering grounded in the call transcripts to see which gave more reliable, less hallucinated responses.
Tailored prompts pull the right medical entities and relations out of messy transcript text, which is what makes the graph useful.
A query box makes it usable by non-technical people, and a pinned LlamaIndex/LangChain environment rebuilds cleanly.

title: Atari Breakout with DQN
summary: A Deep Q-Network agent that learns to play Atari Breakout from pixels, built as a clean, modular, reproducible codebase.

case.problem: Train an agent to play Atari Breakout from raw pixel input using value-based reinforcement learning.
case.data: The Atari Breakout environment — stacked game frames as the agent's state.
case.approach: I implemented a Deep Q-Network from the ground up and structured it as a proper codebase rather than one notebook: a CNN-LSTM Q-network (model.py), the agent and its learning loop (agent.py, train.py), the environment setup (environment.py), a central config (config/config.py), and a separate script to load and evaluate a trained agent (load_and_test_model.py).

methods.why: A convolutional stack reads the frames and an LSTM adds memory across them, so the agent can perceive motion — the ball's direction and speed — not just a single static image.
Value-based RL lets the agent learn purely by playing and improving its action-values, with no labelled data.
A standard, reproducible Breakout environment with frame preprocessing, so runs are comparable and easy to reproduce.
All hyperparameters live in one place, so experiments are repeatable and easy to tweak without touching the training code.
Training and inference are separated and weights are saved, so a trained agent can be reloaded and played back without retraining.

title: ECIU AI Hackathon — LangGraph agent
summary: An agentic LLM workflow modelling an interview + document-retrieval process as an explicit LangGraph StateGraph.

case.problem: Model an interview-and-document-retrieval process as a controllable LLM workflow, rather than a single free-form prompt.
case.data: Interview prompts plus a document corpus the agent retrieves from.
case.approach: Built in ECIU_Hackathon.ipynb as an explicit LangGraph StateGraph: I define nodes for greeting, answering and retrieval, wire them with conditional edges, compile the graph and visualise it. LangChain drives the LLM calls and Pydantic types the state passed between nodes.

methods.why: Representing the flow as nodes and edges makes the agent's control flow visible and debuggable, instead of hidden inside one prompt.
Pydantic enforces the shape of the state moving between nodes, so the graph fails loudly on bad data rather than silently misbehaving.
Conditional edges let the agent branch — e.g. retrieve documents only when a question needs grounding — instead of running every step every time.
Drawing the compiled graph makes the design self-documenting and easy to explain.

title: Hack the Climate — Team Continua
credit: Team project · Team Continua, Nordic Edge
summary: A 5-person team forecasting agricultural nutrient runoff to fight water pollution in the Stavanger–Setesdal region.

case.problem: Reduce water pollution in the Stavanger–Setesdal region by predicting nutrient runoff from agricultural areas — the Nordic Edge "Hack the Climate" challenge, tackled by the 5-person Team Continua.
case.data: Environmental and geographic data for the region.
case.approach: The team paired forecasting with geographic context: LSTM models to predict nutrient runoff over time, DDPG (a continuous-action RL method) to explore interventions, and a FastAPI service on AWS to serve it all, with GIS tying predictions to the map. Built in collaboration with local authorities and the Nordic Edge team.

methods.why: Runoff is a time series driven by weather and land use, so a recurrent model captures how conditions build up over time toward pollution events.
A continuous-action RL method lets us explore what interventions reduce runoff, not just predict it.
Pollution is inherently spatial — tying predictions to the map makes them actionable for local authorities.
Serving the models behind a simple API let the wider Nordic Edge team consume the monitoring solution.

title: Optimizing Apache Spark at Scale
summary: A team study of Hadoop/Spark optimizations on the Yelp reviews dataset for UiS's Data-Intensive Systems course.

case.problem: Learn and apply Hadoop and Apache Spark for distributed analytics, then optimise Spark operations to save time and energy — a project for UiS's Data-Intensive Systems (DAT500) course.
case.data: The public Yelp reviews dataset, used as a large sample workload on a Hadoop/Spark cluster.
case.approach: The team implemented a correct baseline Spark job first, then applied and benchmarked optimisations one at a time — caching, cluster configuration, and code-level changes — measuring each against the baseline. The full method and evaluation are written up in the report.

methods.why: Establishing a correct, unoptimised implementation first means every optimisation can be measured against a fair reference.

methods.ref: Spark cache / persist of reused data
methods.why: Caching DataFrames that are reused avoids recomputation — the biggest single win in our report, roughly halving execution time.
Right-sizing executors and partitions keeps the cluster busy without shuffling more data than necessary.
Restructuring transformations to minimise shuffles and wide dependencies cuts the most expensive stages of the job.

title: Auroville Film Institute
summary: A live WordPress website for the Auroville Film Institute — its diploma programme, workshops and cinema-centric courses.

case.problem: The Auroville Film Institute needed a public website to present its programmes — including the 1-year PG Diploma in Open Space Documentary Arts — along with workshops, news and how to apply.
case.approach: I built and shipped the institute's website on WordPress; it's live in production and serving the current intake. Explore it below.

title: IPL Analysis — R Shiny dashboard
summary: An interactive R Shiny dashboard exploring Indian Premier League cricket data (2008–2019).

case.problem: Make IPL cricket data explorable through an interactive dashboard (a Sparks Foundation internship task).
case.approach: Built in app.R as an R Shiny application over the two datasets, with a reactive UI that filters and visualises the data so patterns across seasons, teams and players can be explored interactively.

methods.why: Shiny's reactive model updates the charts instantly as filters change, making the data explorable rather than a static report.
Combining match-level and ball-by-ball data lets the dashboard answer both season-level trends and fine-grained per-over questions.
Charts across teams, seasons and players surface patterns that a raw table can't.
